Identification.label: Golden head fur
Identification.text: Bat Conservation International describes distinctive gold-colored fur on the head of the giant golden-crowned flying fox.
Identification.source: Bat Conservation International, Acerodon jubatus species account
Identification.studyScope: This character is not sufficient by itself to confirm a distant or silhouetted bat.

Habitat.label: Fig-rich forest foraging
Habitat.text: A fecal-analysis study near Subic Bay reported Ficus seeds as predominant components of the diet, supporting forest fruiting-tree dependence.
Habitat.source: Stier and Mildenstein 2005, Journal of Mammalogy 86:719–728
Habitat.studyScope: These food frequencies are from one studied colony and period, not a universal dietary percentage.

Habitat.label: Habitat and diet

Habitat.source: Bat Conservation International, Giant Golden-crowned Flying Fox

Distribution.label: Luban Island colony reassessed

Distribution.source: Ramos & Nemenzo-Calica (2025), Davao Research Journal 16(2):117–129
Distribution.studyScope: Study notes earlier Acerodon jubatus assignment, revised to possible Pteropus spp.; no definitive taxon identity claimed.

Natural history.label: 2026 nightly movement
Natural history.text: Two tagged golden-crowned flying foxes averaged 18.85 km of nightly linear movement in a Philippine tracking study.
Natural history.source: Constantino et al. (2026), Mammalia 90
Natural history.studyScope: Tracking sample included only two Acerodon jubatus and covered at most 45 nights; not a species-wide movement standard.

Natural history.label: Mixed-colony roosting
Natural history.text: Published species notes report tree roosting, sometimes in colonies with large flying foxes.
Natural history.source: Bat Conservation International, Acerodon jubatus species account
Natural history.studyScope: Mixed-colony observations demand separate species assessment before assigning counts.

Conservation.label: Separate dated Philippine legal listing

Conservation.source: DENR ERDB RISE volume 34 number 1, 2022
Conservation.studyScope: This is a report of two dated distinct systems, not verification of legal amendments after 2022.

Conservation.label: Conservation threats

Conservation.source: Bat Conservation International, Giant Golden-crowned Flying Fox

Identification.text: The original description compares the Mindoro taxon with D. leucopterus and supports its distinct status with mitochondrial sequence data.

Identification.sourceLocation: Original diagnosis, type series, geographic and genetic comparison
Identification.studyScope: Phylogenetic evidence is part of the published diagnosis.

Habitat.label: Study forest
Habitat.text: The original study recorded the species in secondary and primary forest on Mindoro.

Habitat.sourceLocation: Original diagnosis, type series, geographic and genetic comparison
Habitat.studyScope: Forest statements refer to original known localities.

Distribution.label: Original Mindoro collection areas
Distribution.text: The original type series includes Mt. Siburan in western Mindoro and Mt. Halcon in eastern Mindoro.

Identification.label: Downturned muzzle
Identification.text: The broad flattened muzzle ends in a downturned mouth used to graze marine vegetation.
Identification.source: Marsh (2009), Dugong: Dugong dugon, Encyclopedia of Marine Mammals, second edition, pp.332–335
Identification.studyScope: Global external anatomy, not a Philippine occurrence report

Identification.label: Flippers and tail
Identification.text: Dugongs have paddle-like foreflippers, a whale-like fluked tail and no dorsal fin.

Habitat.studyScope: 344 feeding trails measured in Singapore, outside the Philippines; no inference about local Philippine dugong populations.

Habitat.text: The Singapore study associated dugong feeding trails with higher-biomass patches in Halodule–Halophila meadows.
Habitat.source: Ng et al. (2026), Global Ecology and Conservation 69:e04287
Habitat.studyScope: 344 feeding trails measured in Singapore, outside the Philippines; no inference about local Philippine dugong populations.

Habitat.label: Published broad habitat
Habitat.text: MDD summarizes this sirenian across tropical coastal waters of the Indian and western Pacific oceans, including the Philippines. This is a wide distribution summary, not a verified local seagrass record.

Identification.label: Head and ears
Identification.text: A long, narrow snout and small eyes and ears form part of the published external diagnosis.
Identification.source: Rowsey et al. (2022), Journal of Mammalogy 103:1259–1277
Identification.studyScope: Combination of characters; not a visual confirmation from a distant image.

Identification.label: Coat and tail
Identification.text: Dense dark fur covers the body. The visibly haired tail tapers and is shorter than head-and-body length.
Identification.source: Rowsey et al. (2022), Journal of Mammalogy 103:1259–1277
Identification.studyScope: Preserved skin and live appearance can differ.

Identification.label: Published body measures
Identification.text: The type-series comparison reports head-and-body lengths of 131–143 mm and a tail close to 74% of head-and-body length.
Identification.source: Rowsey et al. (2022), Journal of Mammalogy 103:1259–1277
Identification.studyScope: These values describe specimens in the study and are not mandatory cutoffs.

Identification.label: Distinction from Tarsomys and Limnomys
Identification.text: The published comparison uses external proportions and cranial traits, not snout shape alone, to distinguish Baletemys from related Philippine shrew-mice.
Identification.source: Rowsey et al. (2022), Journal of Mammalogy 103:1259–1277
Identification.studyScope: Skull characters need examination of suitable material; the panel is not a field key.

Identification.label: Published taxon-specific note
Identification.text: The mammal database documents a description from lower montane forest of Mount Kampalili in Mindanao; exact specimen coordinates are not published by LIKAS.

Habitat.label: Observed montane habitat
Habitat.text: Study specimens came from old-growth montane and mossy forest on Mt. Kampalili at 1,640 and 1,900 m.
Habitat.source: Rowsey et al. (2022), Journal of Mammalogy 103:1259–1277
Habitat.studyScope: Capture heights are observations, not a complete altitudinal range.

Distribution.label: Documented collection area
Distribution.text: The original description documents two collection localities about six kilometres apart on southern Mt. Kampalili, eastern Mindanao.
Distribution.source: Rowsey et al. (2022), Journal of Mammalogy 103:1259–1277
Distribution.studyScope: The authors discuss potential occurrence elsewhere; broader range is not confirmed.

Distribution.label: Type habitat and occurrence
Distribution.text: The described Kampalili shrew mouse originates from lower montane primary forest on the southern slopes of Mount Kampalili, Mindanao. Its type record was at roughly 1,640 m; this is not a species-wide elevation envelope.
